Wikipedia philosophy phenomenon
The
Wikipedia philosophy phenomenon
, sometimes called the "
Philosophy Game
", is the tendency that clicking the first
hyperlink
in the main text of an
English Wikipedia
article, and then repeating the process for subsequent articles, usually leads to the "
Philosophy
" article.
[
1
]
History
The phenomenon was discovered in 2008 by a teenage
Wikipedian
named Mark J.
[
2
]
[
3
]
The phenomenon received widespread attention from a "fun fact" in the
xkcd
webcomic on 25 May 2011, which led
University of Vermont
researchers Mark Ibrahim,
Christopher Danforth
, and
Peter Sheridan Dodds
to publish a paper on the matter.
[
1
]
The research found that the first link generalises the topic and eventually leads to "Philosophy":
So while a great many [First Link Network] paths flow to "Philosophy" [...], the accumulation is not the result of many articles directly referencing "Philosophy." Instead, first links flow towards "Philosophy" as the ultimate anchor, by generalizing from specific to broad.
[
4
]
In February 2016, the phenomenon was true for 97% of all articles on Wikipedia,
[
5
]
an increase from 94.52% in 2011.
[
6
]
Tools have been developed which map links between articles to find where loops end.
[
3
]
Other languages
Some other language Wikipedias, like the
German
,
French
and
Russian
editions, also led to "Philosophy" like the English Wikipedia. Others, like the
Dutch
and
Japanese
editions, did not.
[
5
]
As of 2017, the concepts with highest
centrality
to first link networks in European language Wikipedias are sciences, such as "Psychology" for Italian Wikipedia,
[
5
]
while East Asian languages are connected by concepts such as
humans
or
Earth
.
[
7
